{{Short description|End of a parliamentary session}}
{{Politics of Canada}}
'''Prorogation''' is the end of a [[parliamentary session]] in the [[Parliament of Canada]] and the parliaments of its provinces and territories. It differs from a [[Recess (motion)|recess]] or [[Adjournment#Parliamentary procedure|adjournment]], which do not end a session; and differs from a complete [[Dissolution of parliament#Canada|dissolution of parliament]], which ends both the session and the entire parliament, requiring an election for the [[House of Commons (Canada)|House of Commons]] in the [[Bicameralism|bicameral]] federal parliament and the singular legislative chamber of the unicameral provincial parliaments.

In the Canadian parliamentary system, the legislature is typically prorogued upon the completion of the agenda set forth in the [[Speech from the throne|Speech from the Throne]] and remains in recess until the monarch or [[Governor General of Canada|governor general]], in the federal sphere, or [[Lieutenant Governor (Canada)|lieutenant governor]], in a province, summons parliamentarians. Since 2008, when the Parliament of Canada was [[2008–2009 Canadian parliamentary dispute|prorogued for political reasons]] in lieu of dissolution, followed by a [[40th Canadian Parliament#2nd session and prorogation|second use by the same prime minister in 2009]], prorogation has been the subject of ongoing discussion among academics, the Canadian public, and their political representatives.

==Mechanism==
{{further|Parliament of Canada#Term}}
It is, according to the [[constitution of Canada]], the [[Monarchy of Canada|Canadian monarch's]] [[royal prerogative]] to prorogue the legislatures, though this is usually done for the federal parliament by the sovereign's federal representative, the [[Governor General of Canada]], and always for the provincial parliaments by the monarch's provincial representatives, the [[Lieutenant Governor (Canada)|lieutenant governors]]. Like all such actions of the sovereign and governors, this is exclusively done on the advice of the relevant prime minister who holds the [[Confidence and supply|confidence]] of the House of Commons.

A [[Legislative session|parliamentary session]] lasts until a prorogation, after which, without ceremony in recent years, one or both chambers of the legislature cease all legislative business until the governor general or lieutenant governor issues a proclamation calling for a new session to begin. For the federal parliament, except for the election of a speaker for the House of Commons and his or her claiming of that house's privileges, the same procedures for the opening of parliament are again followed.

Prorogation is a routine action, including in "situations where governments need to stop and refocus." At the same time, arbitrary use of the power of prorogation can "[unbalance] the very fragile balance of power that exists between the different parts of government." What is paramount is that the legislature be recalled so the opposition can hold the cabinet to account for its actions,<ref name=GlobeIbbitson>{{cite news| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/silent-parliaments-muted-outrage-the-problem-with-prorogation/article4617327/| last=Ibbitson| first=John| title=Silent parliaments, muted outrage: The problem with prorogation| date=October 17, 2012| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| access-date=October 17, 2012}}</ref> a task central to the functioning of [[responsible government]].<ref name=Citizen>{{cite news| url=https://ottawacitizen.com/news/Jean+decision+prorogue+Parliament+2008+influenced+McGuinty/7399741/story.html| last=Cobb| first=Chris| title=How Michaëlle Jean's decision to prorogue Parliament in 2008 influenced McGuinty| date=October 16, 2012| newspaper=Ottawa Citizen| access-date=October 21, 2012}}</ref>

==History==
In the 19th and early 20th centuries, prorogations in Canada lasted at least half of any given year. Parliament would typically be in session from February until June, give or take a few months, and would be prorogued for the remainder of the year, giving Members of Parliament the opportunity to spend a substantial amount of time in their home [[Electoral district (Canada)|ridings]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.worldissues360.com/index.php/what-is-prorogation-9838| last=Scott| first=Cameron| title=What is Prorogation?| date=October 17, 2010| publisher= Helium Inc.| access-date=November 10, 2013}}</ref> Only when vast amounts of legislation needed to be debated and passed during the [[World War II|Second World War]] did parliament begin to sit for longer sessions. This was followed by an expansion of the government's role in Canadian life through the 1950s and 1960s, requiring even shorter prorogations.<ref name=Moore-1>{{cite journal| last1=Moore| first1=Christopher| title=A (pro)rogue's gallery| journal=[[Canada's History]]| issue=April–May 2010| pages=45–46}}</ref> Additionally, the advent of modern communication tools and air travel rendered long prorogations even more unnecessary; Members of Parliament may contact their home ridings whenever they want and can visit their home ridings during adjournments. Today, sessions of parliament still last about one year each, but the prorogation in between sessions is often only a few days and new sessions are started more for organizational or political reasons than for the purpose of giving members of parliament time away. Between 1867 and 2010 the average period of prorogation was 151 days. However, in the 30 year period between 1980 and 2010, the average was just 22 days.<ref name=Halted>{{cite news| title=Halted in mid-debate| newspaper=The Economist| publisher=Economist Group| location=London| date=January 7, 2010| url=http://www.economist.com/world/americas/displaystory.cfm?STORY_ID=15211862| issn=0013-0613| access-date=February 3, 2010}}</ref>
[[File:Frederick Temple Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava by George Frederic Watts.jpg|thumb|upright|Governor General [[Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|the Earl of Dufferin]]]]

In 1873, during the [[2nd Canadian Parliament]], [[Prime Minister of Canada|Prime Minister]] Sir [[John A. Macdonald]] advised Governor General [[Frederick Hamilton-Temple-Blackwood, 1st Marquess of Dufferin and Ava|the Earl of Dufferin]] to prorogue parliament in order to stop the work of a committee investigating Macdonald's involvement in the [[Pacific Scandal]]. While the Governor General did reluctantly accept advice to prorogue parliament, he insisted that the prorogation be limited to a period of ten weeks, and that a commission be appointed to continue the hearings, which would report to parliament when it reconvened. When parliament returned and the commission presented their findings, Macdonald was [[Censure#Canada|censured]] and had to resign.<ref>{{cite news| last=Valpy| first=Michael| author-link=Michael Valpy| title=There's no hint whether prorogation came with strings attached| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=December 5, 2008| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/servlet/story/RTGAM.20081205.wparlgg05/BNStory/politics/home| access-date=December 5, 2008| location=Toronto}}</ref> According to [[Christopher Moore (Canadian historian)|Christopher Moore]], it was at this point that the relationship between [[backbencher]]s and the prime minister began an evolution; "MacDonald himself became one of the inventors of the 'party machine'—the party as a disciplined, centralized, loyal team that would not dare to turn on him as it had in 1873." By the mid-20th century, parliamentary caucuses were being told by their leaders that they had "no right to question what a leader did or said".<ref name=Moore-1 />
[[File:Michaëlle Jean 11-11-2007.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Governor General [[Michaëlle Jean]]]]

In 2002, Governor General [[Adrienne Clarkson]] accepted Prime Minister [[Jean Chrétien]]'s advice to prorogue parliament, allowing Chrétien to avoid tabling a report to the House of Commons public accounts committee regarding the [[sponsorship scandal]] that surrounded [[Liberal Party of Canada|Chrétien's party]] at the time.<ref>{{cite news| last=Foot| first=Richard| title=Only In Canada: Harper's Prorogation is a Canadian thing| newspaper=Montreal Gazette| date=January 18, 2010| url=https://montrealgazette.com/news/Only+Canada+Harper+prorogation+Canadian+thing/2448571/story.html| access-date=December 1, 2010}}</ref> After parliament was again summoned, investigations into the scandal continued, Chrétien stepped down as Prime Minister in December of the following year, and the Liberal party was reduced to a [[minority government]] in the [[2004 Canadian federal election|subsequent election]].

A prorogation of parliament took place on December 4, 2008, when Prime Minister [[Stephen Harper]] advised Governor General [[Michaëlle Jean]] to do so after the [[Opposition (parliamentary)|opposition]] [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal]] and [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic]] parties formed a coalition with the support of the [[Bloc Québécois]] party and threatened to vote non-confidence in the sitting [[Minority governments in Canada|minority government]], precipitating [[2008–2009 Canadian parliamentary dispute|a parliamentary dispute]]. The Governor General, however, did not grant her prime minister's request until after two hours of consultation with various constitutional experts. Upon the end of her tenure as vicereine, Jean revealed to the Canadian Press that the delay was partly to "send a message—and for people to understand that this warranted reflection".<ref>{{cite news| last=Panetta| first=Alexander| title=Michaëlle Jean had hidden message in prorogation crisis| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=September 28, 2010| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/michalle-jean-had-hidden-message-in-prorogation-crisis/article1730587/| access-date=September 30, 2010| location=Toronto}}</ref><ref name=Queen>{{cite news| last=Ibbitson| first=John| author-link=John Ibbitson| title=Stephen Harper pondered appeal to Queen over prorogation| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=September 30, 2010| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/stephen-harper-pondered-appeal-to-queen-over-prorogation/article1733882/| access-date=September 30, 2010| location=Toronto}}</ref> It was also at the same time said by [[Peter H. Russell]], one of those from whom Jean sought advice, that Canadians ought not regard as an automatic [[Rubber stamp (politics)|rubber stamp]] the Governor General's decision to accept Harper's advice concerning prorogation; Russell disclosed that Jean granted the prorogation on two conditions: parliament would reconvene soon and, when it did, the Cabinet would present a proposed budget, a vote on which is a confidence matter.<ref name=Citizen /> This, Russell said, set a precedent that would prevent future prime ministers from advising the prorogation of parliament "for any length of time for any reason".<ref name=Russell>{{cite news| title=PM gave Jean pledges in prorogation crisis| publisher=CBC| date=October 2, 2010| url=http://ca.news.yahoo.com/s/cbc/101002/topstories/politics_harper_jean_prorogation| access-date=October 17, 2010| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101008150053/http://ca.news.yahoo.com/s/cbc/101002/topstories/politics_harper_jean_prorogation| archive-date=October 8, 2010}}</ref><ref name=Russel2>{{cite news| last=Elliott| first=Louise| title=PM gave Jean pledges in prorogation crisis|  publisher=CBC| date=October 2, 2010| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/pm-gave-jean-pledges-in-prorogation-crisis-1.969491| access-date=November 13, 2010}}</ref>  Nelson Wiseman, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, wrote of Harper that "no Prime Minister has so abused the power to prorogue".<ref>{{cite web|last=Wiseman|first=Nelson|title=The use, misuse, and abuse of prorogation|url=http://www.thehilltimes.ca/page/view/wiseman-03-01-2010|work=The Hill Times}}</ref>

Harper [[40th Canadian Parliament#2nd Session and prorogation|again advised the Governor General to prorogue parliament]] on December 30, 2009. The Prime Minister stated that this was to keep parliament in recess for the duration of the [[2010 Winter Olympics|XXI Olympic Winter Games]] to be held in [[Vancouver]], [[British Columbia]], in February 2010. The move, however, was suspected by opposition Members of Parliament to be a way for Harper to avoid ongoing investigations into [[Canadian Afghan detainee issue|the Afghan detainees affair]].

In October 2012, [[Lieutenant Governor of Ontario]] [[David Onley]], on the advice of [[Premier of Ontario|Premier]] [[Dalton McGuinty]], who headed a minority government, prorogued the [[Ontario Legislature]], with McGuinty announcing, at the same time, he would, after a new party leader was selected, resign both as premier and leader of the [[Ontario Liberal Party]]. Liberal House Leader [[John Milloy]] later stated that prorogation was necessary because an impasse was reached with labour leaders and the opposition over plans to freeze all public sector wages. The opposition charged that it was done to dodge negative publicity over the investigation and criminal probe into the [[Ornge|Ornge Air affair]], as well as the controversial decision to halt construction of two [[gas-fired power plant]]s during the [[2011 Ontario general election|previous election]] and the subsequent threats by the opposition to vote on finding Cabinet ministers in [[Contempt of Parliament]] for withholding from the legislature information related to halting the projects.<ref>{{cite news| author=Canadian Press| title=Ontario prorogation halts key hearings, bills| publisher=CBC News| date=October 16, 2012| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ontario-prorogation-halts-key-hearings-bills-1.1156011| access-date=October 16, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| last=Howlett| first=Karen| title=McGuinty's exit plan drawn up in shadow of rising scandal| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=October 16, 2012| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/mcguintys-exit-plan-drawn-up-in-shadow-of-rising-scandal/article4617420/| access-date=October 16, 2012}}</ref> In early 2013, Onley explained in an interview conducted by the ''[[Toronto Star]]'' that, though he and McGuinty discussed the matter, among others, before he granted the prorogation, he ultimately could only follow the constitution and adhere to the principles of [[responsible government]]; only if the premier were "trying to subvert democracy" could Onley have refused the advice and, as Onley put it, "something that's politically controversial doesn't fit that category. Doesn't even come close... It's up to the politicians to work out the political process, the political decision-making that is behind prorogation—and the fallout after prorogation." On the subject of the lack of a date on which the legislature would be summoned to return, the Lieutenant Governor said he had no guide; the legislature's standing orders outline that a specific date must be set, but the Legislative Assembly Act does not, and precedents are inconsistent.

On August 18, 2020, Prime Minister [[Justin Trudeau]] asked Governor General [[Julie Payette]] to prorogue parliament until September 23 amidst the aftermath of the [[WE Charity scandal]] and [[cabinet shuffle]]. His request was granted.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trudeau prorogues Parliament — what exactly does that mean? - National {{!}} Globalnews.ca|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/7283685/trudeau-prorogues-parliament-explained/|access-date=2021-09-14|website=Global News|language=en-US}}</ref>

On January 6, 2025, Prime Minister Trudeau asked Governor General [[Mary Simon]] to prorogue parliament until March 24 due to mounting pressure from his own caucus to resign while leading a [[minority government]] under threat from other parties to unseat his government through an imminent [[non-confidence motion]]. His request was granted, and Trudeau subsequently announced that he will resign as prime minister when his Liberal Party picks a successor.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trudeau to resign as prime minister after Liberal leadership race {{!}} cbcnews.ca|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/trudeau-news-conference-1.7423680|access-date=2025-01-06|website=CBC News|language=en-CA}}</ref> The decision was subject to [[#2025 legal challenge|a legal challenge]] and upheld in the [[Federal Court (Canada)|Federal Court]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Major |first=Darren |date=March 6, 2025 |title=Court dismisses legal challenge to Trudeau's prorogation decision |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/court-challenge-prorogation-dismissed-1.7477263 |access-date=March 6, 2025 |work=[[CBC News]]}}</ref>

==Calls for reform==
[[Image:Protests against prorogation in Vancouver (2).jpg|thumb|A march in [[Vancouver]] against the second prorogation of the 40th Parliament]]

The prorogations of the federal parliament in 2008 and 2009, and the speculation that such use of the royal prerogative had been advised by the sitting prime minister for political purposes, triggered [[2010 Canada anti-prorogation protests|protests]] in various cities across the country through early 2010.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/thousands-protest-parliament-s-suspension-1.866970| title=Thousands protest Parliament's suspension| publisher=CBC| date=January 23, 2010| access-date=January 24, 2010| url-status=live| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100125061406/http://www.cbc.ca/politics/story/2010/01/23/prorogue-protests.html| archive-date=January 25, 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/pm-shuts-down-parliament-until-march-1.829800| title=PM shuts down Parliament until March| publisher=CBC| date=December 31, 2009| access-date=December 31, 2009}}</ref>

Within a week after the latter prorogation, the [[non-partisan|multi-partisan]] organization [[Fair Vote Canada]] had gathered the signatures of 132 political scientists to a letter condemning the move and advocating for [[electoral reform]].<ref name=Halted /><ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.fairvote.ca/en/fvc-news/132-political-scientists-call-for-action-on-democratic-deficit| title=132 political scientists call for action on the democratic deficit| publisher=Fair Vote Canada| date=January 5, 2010| access-date=February 5, 2010| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100203161559/http://www.fairvote.ca/en/fvc-news/132-political-scientists-call-for-action-on-democratic-deficit| archive-date=February 3, 2010}}</ref> [[New Democratic Party (Canada)|New Democratic Party]] (NDP) leader [[Jack Layton]] called on January 20 and 23, 2010, for limits to prorogation, stating his party would put forward proposed legislative changes that would require a majority vote of MPs for the prorogation of parliament.<ref name=CBCLayton>{{cite news|title=Layton calls for limits on powers to prorogue| publisher=CBC| date=January 20, 2010| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/layton-calls-for-limits-on-powers-to-prorogue-1.954224| access-date=February 2, 2010| url-status=live| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100123182320/http://www.cbc.ca/politics/story/2010/01/20/ndp-prorogue-limits.html| archive-date=January 23, 2010 }}</ref><ref name=cbc1>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/thousands-protest-parliament-s-suspension-1.866970| title=Thousands protest Parliament's suspension| date=January 23, 2010| publisher=CBC| access-date=January 24, 2010| url-status=live| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100125061406/http://www.cbc.ca/politics/story/2010/01/23/prorogue-protests.html| archive-date=January 25, 2010 }}</ref> Five days later, [[Liberal Party of Canada]] leader [[Michael Ignatieff]] also called for limits to the ability of the prime minister to advise the prorogation of parliament,<ref name=CBCLayton /> his plan requiring the consent of the [[House of Commons of Canada]], following ten days written notice and debate.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/liberals-unveil-prorogation-proposal-of-their-own-1.951457| title=Liberals unveil prorogation proposal of their own| date=January 25, 2010| publisher=Canadian Broadcasting Corporation| access-date=January 29, 2010}}</ref> Ignatieff brushed off questions about the constitutionality of the proposed changes, saying if new rules are established, governors general "will respect those constitutional conventions" as they always have, adding: "The problem is not with the governor general. The problem is with the Prime Minister of Canada."<ref>{{cite news| last=Greenaway| first=Norma| title=Opposition seeks to limit Harper's prorogation powers| newspaper=National Post| date=January 25, 2010| url=https://nationalpost.com/most-popular/story.html?id=2481830| access-date=January 29, 2010}}{{dead link|date=October 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| last=Leblanc| first=Daniel| title=Opposition pushes for new rules on prorogation| newspaper=The Globe and Mail| date=January 28, 2010| url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/prorogation/opposition-pushes-for-new-rules-on-prorogation/article1443657/| access-date=January 29, 2010| location=Toronto}}</ref> These proposals echoed the arrangements within the [[Long Parliament]] of England, between 1640 and 1648, which could only be dissolved with the agreement of its members.<ref>{{citation| author=Charles I| author-link=Charles I of England| publication-date=May 11, 1641| title=Act against Dissolving the Long Parliament without its own Consent| publication-place=Westminster| publisher=King's Printer| url=http://home.freeuk.net/don-aitken/ast/c1.html#198| access-date=June 15, 2010}}</ref>

The NDP presented a [[Motion (parliamentary procedure)|motion]] to the House of Commons requesting the prime minister not advise the governor general to prorogue parliament for more than seven days unless approved by a majority vote by the lower house. The motion passed on March 17, 2010, by a vote of 139 to 135,<ref>{{cite news| title=Motion to limit PM's prorogation power passes| publisher=CBC| date=March 17, 2010| url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/motion-to-limit-pm-s-prorogation-power-passes-1.899822?ref=rss| access-date=March 20, 2010}}</ref> but motions are not binding. Five days later, Liberal, [[Bloc Québécois]], and NDP MPs used their majority in the Commons committee in charge of MPs' privilege and rules to approve an official review of the convention of prorogation, which could require a prime minister to seek approval from the House before asking the governor general to end a parliamentary session.<ref>{{cite news| last=Naumetz| first=Tim| title=Opposition parties push for a showdown over Afghan documents, PM's power to prorogue| newspaper=The Hill Times| date=March 22, 2010| url=http://www.hilltimes.com/page/view/opposition-03-22-2010| access-date=March 21, 2010}}</ref>

In October 2010, Peter Russell said to the press that he had organized for February 2011, with the support of Governor General [[David Johnston (governor general)|David Johnston]], a meeting of constitutional scholars, historians, and government officials from various countries in the hopes of finding a consensus on how the royal prerogative should be used in future scenarios similar to that which took place at the end of 2008.<ref name=Russell /><ref name=Russel2/> Following the prorogation of the [[Legislative Assembly of Ontario]] in October 2012, Daniel Weinstock, a professor of law at [[McGill University]], opined that there may be a need for new procedures "to discipline power", limiting in all of Canada's jurisdictions the royal prerogative to prorogue parliament, among other legislative procedures.<ref name=GlobeIbbitson /> At the same time, some journalists, such as [[Norman Spector]] and [[Andrew Coyne]], lamented the abuse of the power of prorogation and its negative effect on democracy in Canada.<ref name=Citizen/><ref>{{cite news| url=https://nationalpost.com/opinion/andrew-coyne-mcguinty-prorogation-shows-canadas-parliamentary-democracy-becoming-increasingly-ceremonial| last=Coyne| first=Andrew| author-link=Andrew Coyne| title=McGuinty prorogation shows Canada's parliamentary democracy becoming increasingly ceremonial| date=October 19, 2012| newspaper=National Post| access-date=October 21, 2012| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021100500/http://fullcomment.nationalpost.com/2012/10/19/andrew-coyne-mcguinty-prorogation-shows-canadas-parliamentary-democracy-becoming-increasingly-ceremonial/| archive-date=October 21, 2012| url-status=live}}</ref> However, the [[Federal Court of Canada]], in a 2009 ruling, found that tampering with the Crown's prerogatives could not be done via normal legislation, requiring instead an amendment to the constitution pursuant to [[Constitution Act, 1982#Amending the Constitution|Section 41 of the Constitution Act, 1982]].<ref>{{cite conference| url=http://www.queensu.ca/iigr/conf/Arch/2010/ConferenceOnTheCrown/CrownConferencePapers/The_Crown_and_the_Constitutio1.pdf| title=The Crown and the Constitution: Sustaining Democracy?| last=Smith| first=David E.| conference=The Crown in Canada: Present Realities and Future Options| date=June 10, 2010| conference-url=http://www.queensu.ca/iigr/conf/Arch/2010/ConferenceOnTheCrown.html| publisher=Queen's University| location=Ottawa| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017024753/http://www.queensu.ca/iigr/conf/Arch/2010/ConferenceOnTheCrown/CrownConferencePapers/The_Crown_and_the_Constitutio1.pdf| archive-date=October 17, 2013}}, referencing 
{{cite court| litigants=Conacher v. Canada (Prime Minister)| vol=2009 FC 920| court=Federal Court of Canada| date=17 September 2009| url=http://www.canlii.org/en/ca/fct/doc/2009/2009fc920/2009fc920.html}}</ref>

[[Christopher Moore (Canadian historian)|Christopher Moore]] opined in ''[[Canada's History]]'' that "no great web of new [[legislation]] or [[constitution]]al procedure is needed to rein in the abuse of prime ministerial powers. Other parliaments around the world regularly see party leaders and prime ministers dumped when their own backbenchers and prime ministers {{sic}} <!-- Surely the dual mention of prime ministers is a mistake --> grow tired of them. If our premiers and prime ministers knew that legislatures would rebuke them for abusing parliament (as did the backbenchers in the legislature of 1873), we would not have to worry about rogue prorogations."<ref name=Moore-1/>

== 2025 legal challenge ==
Until the [[2024–2025 Canadian political crisis]], little discussion took on the significance of the 2019 UK case of ''[[R (Miller) v The Prime Minister and Cherry v Advocate General for Scotland|R (Miller) v The Prime Minister]],'' which overturned a prorogation, on similar Canadian events.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=Mach |first=Jessica |date=February 15, 2025 |title=Federal court chief justice questions stance that UK ruling doesn't apply to prorogation lawsuit |url=https://www.canadianlawyermag.com/news/general/federal-court-chief-justice-questions-stance-that-uk-ruling-doesnt-apply-to-prorogation-lawsuit/391270 |access-date=March 6, 2025 |work=[[Canadian Lawyer Magazine]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite BAILII|litigants=R (on the application of Miller) v The Prime Minister''; ''Cherry and Others v Advocate General for Scotland|court=UKSC|year=2019|num=41|date=24 September 2019}}</ref>  In January 2025, Prime Minister's [[Justin Trudeau]]'s prorogation of the House of Commons was challenged in the [[Federal Court (Canada)|Federal Court]] citing ''Miller II''.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=January 18, 2025 |title=Judge agrees to expedite legal challenge of Trudeau's move to prorogue Parliament |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/article/judge-agrees-to-expedite-legal-challenge-of-trudeaus-move-to-prorogue-parliament/ |access-date=January 18, 2025 |work=[[CTV News]] |agency=[[The Canadian Press]]}}</ref> During arguments, government lawyers argued that ''Miller II''<nowiki/>'s holding that the constitutional role of Parliament by prorogation could be distinguished because of the unique scenario with the British Parliament's role in relation to an imminently approaching Brexit. Government lawyers also argued that unlike the unwritten [[Constitution of the United Kingdom]], which was silent on required Parliamentary sittings, [[Section 5 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|Section 5 of the ''Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms'']] required annual sittings providing a check on the power.<ref name=":2" /> In March 2025, Federal Court Chief Justice [[Paul S. Crampton|Paul Crampton]] held that the decision to prorogue was [[Justiciability|justiciable]], but ultimately declined to adopt ''Miller II.''.<ref>''MacKinnon v. Canada'', [https://www.canlii.org/en/ca/fct/doc/2025/2025fc422/2025fc422.html 2025 FC 422], at para 169.</ref> He ruled the applicants had failed to prove that Trudeau had breached the ''Charter'' or any other legal limits on the power, and dismissed the case.<ref name=":0" />
